Summary and 
Key terms
17
• Direct reversal repair is to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers on the same DNA 
strand by photoreactivation using energy from visible light.
• Base-excision repair is to recognize specific lesions (deamination) and repair at AP 
(apyrimidinic or apurinic) site. 
• Nucleotide-excision repair is to recognize and remove an oligonucleotide 
containing the lesion. 
• Mismatch repair distinguishes between parental DNA and newly synthesized DNA 
and specifically removes mismatched bases from newly synthesized DNA strands. 
• Translesion DNA synthesis repairs lesions by specialized DNA polymerases that are 
capable of replicating DNA across from a site of DNA damage.
• Double-strand breaks are repaired by recombination to rejoin the damaged 
strands, either by nonhomologous end joining of the broken ends or by 
homologous recombination with an undamaged chromosome.

candidates.full_text:
Roles of introns (2)
15
• Although introns are excised from completed mRNAs, they have many other 
important biological roles. 
• Second, introns contain regulatory sequences that control gene expression, which 
is critical to cell behavior. 
– Since all cells in an organism contain the same genes, regulated differences in 
gene expression determine the difference between one type of cell and 
another.
– Transcription is regulated by transcriptional regulatory sequences that reside 
in a variety of locations: upstream of genes, distant locations in the genome, 
or within genes (gene’s 1st intron or 5’ UTR of 1st exon). 
– Approximately 10–20% of the human genome consists of sequences that act 
to regulate gene expression.

contains about twice as much protein as DNA.

Summary _The Structure of Eukaryotic Genes 
19
 Gene
 Exon, Intron
 RNA splicing
 5’ and 3’ UTR (untranslated region)

• Most eukaryotic genes have a split structure in which segments of coding sequence 
(exons) are interrupted by noncoding sequences (introns). 
• The exons include 5’ UTR and 3’ UTR regions at both the 5’ and 3’ ends of the mRNA 
that are not translated into protein, respectively.

Roles of introns (2)
15
• Although introns are excised from completed mRNAs, they have many other 
important biological roles. 
• Second, introns contain regulatory sequences that control gene expression, which 
is critical to cell behavior. 
– Since all cells in an organism contain the same genes, regulated differences in 
gene expression determine the difference between one type of cell and 
another.
– Transcription is regulated by transcriptional regulatory sequences that reside 
in a variety of locations: upstream of genes, distant locations in the genome, 
or within genes (gene’s 1st intron or 5’ UTR of 1st exon). 
– Approximately 10–20% of the human genome consists of sequences that act 
to regulate gene expression.

29
• Simple-sequence repeats consists of tandem arrays of up to thousands of copies 
of short sequences, ranging 1~500 nucleotides. 
– In Drosophila, tandem repeats of the seven-nucleotide unit ACAAACT
– In humans, A/T-rich sequence of 171 bp known as α-satellite DNA. 
– These sequences are repeated millions of times per genome, accounting for 
~40% of total genomic DNA in Drosophila and ~10% in humans
• Simple-sequence DNAs are not transcribed and do not convey functional genetic 
information.

Key terms
17
• Direct reversal repair is to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers on the same DNA 
strand by photoreactivation using energy from visible light.
• Base-excision repair is to recognize specific lesions (deamination) and repair at AP 
(apyrimidinic or apurinic) site. 
• Nucleotide-excision repair is to recognize and remove an oligonucleotide 
containing the lesion. 
• Mismatch repair distinguishes between parental DNA and newly synthesized DNA 
and specifically removes mismatched bases from newly synthesized DNA strands. 
• Translesion DNA synthesis repairs lesions by specialized DNA polymerases that are 
capable of replicating DNA across from a site of DNA damage.
• Double-strand breaks are repaired by recombination to rejoin the damaged 
strands, either by nonhomologous end joining of the broken ends or by 
homologous recombination with an undamaged chromosome.

2.3. Mismatch repair 
8
• During DNA replication, mismatched bases are removed by the proofreading 
activity of DNA polymerase.
• However, the ones that are missed are subject to later correction by the 
mismatch repair system, which scans newly replicated DNA. 
 If a mismatch is found, the enzymes of the mismatch repair system are able 
to identify and excise the mismatched base specifically from the newly 
replicated DNA strand, allowing the error to be corrected and the original 
sequence restored.
• The mismatch repair system distinguishes between parental DNA and newly 
synthesized DNA.

5
• Excision repair is a more general means of repairing a wide variety of chemical 
alterations to DNA. 
 The damaged DNA is recognized and removed, either as free bases or as 
nucleotides. The resulting gap is then filled in by synthesis of a new DNA 
strand, using the undamaged complementary strand as a template. 
• Three types of excision repair 
1) Base-excision repair
2) Nucleotide-excision repair 
3) Mismatch repair

Summary and 
Key terms
17
• Direct reversal repair is to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers on the same DNA 
strand by photoreactivation using energy from visible light.
• Base-excision repair is to recognize specific lesions (deamination) and repair at AP 
(apyrimidinic or apurinic) site. 
• Nucleotide-excision repair is to recognize and remove an oligonucleotide 
containing the lesion. 
• Mismatch repair distinguishes between parental DNA and newly synthesized DNA 
and specifically removes mismatched bases from newly synthesized DNA strands. 
• Translesion DNA synthesis repairs lesions by specialized DNA polymerases that are 
capable of replicating DNA across from a site of DNA damage.
• Double-strand breaks are repaired by recombination to rejoin the damaged 
strands, either by nonhomologous end joining of the broken ends or by 
homologous recombination with an undamaged chromosome.

Translesion DNA synthesis
11
• The direct reversal and excision repair systems act to correct DNA damage 
before replication, so that replicative DNA synthesis can proceed using an 
undamaged DNA strand as a template. 
• Cells possess several specialized DNA polymerases that is capable of 
replicating across a site of DNA damage.
 The replication of damaged DNA by these specialized polymerases 
= Translesion DNA synthesis
• Translesion DNA synthesis provides an alternative mechanism by which 
the cell can bypass DNA damage at the replication fork, which can then 
be corrected after replication is complete.

Summary and 
Key terms
28
• Programmed DNA rearrangements of immunoglobulin and T cell receptor genes 
play a critical role in development of the vertebrate immune system.
– Rearrangement of V(D)J regions in light and heavy chain of immunoglobulin. 
– Recombination between V(D)J segments in α and β chain of T cell receptor. 
– V(D)J recombination by RAG1/RAG2 introducing a double-strand break 
between the V(D) coding sequence and RS sequence, accompanied by 
nonhomologous end-joining and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase for 
nucleotide deletions and additions, respectively.
• Additional diversity is provided to immunoglobulin genes by class switch 
recombination and somatic hypermutation.

How can DNA strand be synthesized?
7
• Important points to understand DNA replication
1. Two complementary strands of double-helical DNA run in opposite 
(antiparallel) directions. 
2. DNA polymerase catalyzes the polymerization of dNTPs only in the 5′ to 3′ 
direction. 
• One strand is synthesized in a continuous manner in the same direction in 
which the replication fork moves (in the direction of overall DNA replication) 
 the leading strand
• The other strand is formed from short (1–3 kb), discontinuous pieces of DNA 
that are synthesized backward to the direction of replication fork movement 
 the lagging strand
– Okazaki fragments: Small pieces of newly synthesized DNA 
– DNA ligase: join Okazaki fragments and form a new intact DNA strand

Key 
terms
25
• DNA polymerases synthesize DNA in the 5′  3′ direction by the addition of dNTP to a 
preformed RNA primer.
 The leading strand is synthesized in a continuous manner at the replication fork. 
 The lagging strand is formed by the joining of small Okazaki fragments that are synthesized 
backward of replication.
• DNA polymerases and various other proteins (helicase, primase, single-strand DNA-
binding proteins, clamp-loading protein, sliding-clamp proteins, topoisomerase) act in a 
coordinated manner to synthesize DNA. 
• DNA polymerases increase the accuracy of replication both by selecting the correct base
for insertion and by proofreading newly synthesized DNA to eliminate mismatched bases. 
• DNA replication starts at origins of replication, which contain binding sites for proteins 
that initiate the process. 
• Telomeric repeat sequences are maintained by the action of a reverse transcriptase 
(telomerase) that carries its own template RNA.

candidates.full_text:
How can DNA strand be synthesized?
7
• Important points to understand DNA replication
1. Two complementary strands of double-helical DNA run in opposite 
(antiparallel) directions. 
2. DNA polymerase catalyzes the polymerization of dNTPs only in the 5′ to 3′ 
direction. 
• One strand is synthesized in a continuous manner in the same direction in 
which the replication fork moves (in the direction of overall DNA replication) 
 the leading strand
• The other strand is formed from short (1–3 kb), discontinuous pieces of DNA 
that are synthesized backward to the direction of replication fork movement 
 the lagging strand
– Okazaki fragments: Small pieces of newly synthesized DNA 
– DNA ligase: join Okazaki fragments and form a new intact DNA strand

Summary and 
Key 
terms
25
• DNA polymerases synthesize DNA in the 5′  3′ direction by the addition of dNTP to a 
preformed RNA primer.
 The leading strand is synthesized in a continuous manner at the replication fork. 
 The lagging strand is formed by the joining of small Okazaki fragments that are synthesized 
backward of replication.
• DNA polymerases and various other proteins (helicase, primase, single-strand DNA-
binding proteins, clamp-loading protein, sliding-clamp proteins, topoisomerase) act in a 
coordinated manner to synthesize DNA. 
• DNA polymerases increase the accuracy of replication both by selecting the correct base
for insertion and by proofreading newly synthesized DNA to eliminate mismatched bases. 
• DNA replication starts at origins of replication, which contain binding sites for proteins 
that initiate the process. 
• Telomeric repeat sequences are maintained by the action of a reverse transcriptase 
(telomerase) that carries its own template RNA.

between cysteine residues.

sequence.
• Protein sequences are now usually deduced from the sequences of mRNAs, and 
the complete amino acid sequences of over 100,000 proteins have been 
established.

• In 1953 Frederick Sanger was the first to determine the complete amino acid 
sequence of a protein, the hormone insulin.

• Protein sequences are now usually deduced from the sequences of mRNAs, and 
the complete amino acid sequences of over 100,000 proteins have been 
established.

RNA Is Synthesized by RNA Polymerases

RNA polymerase: catalyzes polymerization of ribonucleoside 5′-

triphosphates (NTPs) as directed by a DNA template, always in the 5′ to 3′ 
direction.

-
The bacterial RNA polymerase core has five subunits of four types: α₂ββ′ω.
-
The σ factor binds the core to form the holoenzyme and directs it to specific promoters.
-
Alternative σ factors direct RNA polymerase to different promoters under different 
conditions.

The α subunit of the polymerase is 
colored green, with β blue, β' pink, 
and ω yellow.

candidates.full_text:
Summary _The Structure of Eukaryotic Genes 
19
 Gene
 Exon, Intron
 RNA splicing
 5’ and 3’ UTR (untranslated region)
 Nested genes
 Transcriptional regulatory elements
 Alternative splicing
• Most eukaryotic genes have a split structure in which segments of coding sequence 
(exons) are interrupted by noncoding sequences (introns). 
• The exons include 5’ UTR and 3’ UTR regions at both the 5’ and 3’ ends of the mRNA 
that are not translated into protein, respectively. 
• Although they are removed from mRNAs, introns have multiple functions.
1. Some proteins or RNAs as nested genes are encoded within introns.
2. Introns contain transcriptional regulatory sequences that control gene expression.
3. Introns allow alternative splicing.
• Key terms

Regulation of transcriptional elongation (Figure 7.17)
CTD: 7aa-52 in human
Transcription is initiated following 
phosphorylation of the RNA 
polymerase II C-terminal domain 
(CTD) at serine-5 by TFIIH.
Factors involved in the initial stages 
of mRNA processing associate with 
the phosphorylated CTD. 
In addition, negative regulatory 
factors (NELF and DSIF) associate 
with the polymerase and cause the 
polymerase to pause within about 50 
nucleotides of the transcription start 
site. DRB sensitivity-inducing factor
Continuation of transcription 
(productive elongation) results from 
the phosphorylation of NELF, DSIF, 
and serine-2 of the polymerase CTD 
by P-TEFb. Phosphorylated NELF 
dissociates from the complex, and 
additional factors required for 
elongation and processing associate 
with the polymerase.
‘stalled’(정체/멈춤)

– DNA is tightly bound to small basic proteins (histones) that package the DNA in an orderly 
way in cell nucleus. 
– In a human cell, total DNA (2 m length) fits into a nucleus (5–10 μm diameter) 
Chromosome Numbers of Eukaryotic Cells

• Eukaryotes

the complete amino acid sequences of over 100,000 proteins have been

candidates.full_text:
DNA repair
3
• Because DNA uniquely serves as a permanent copy of the cell genome, changes in 
its structure are of much greater consequence than are alterations in other cell 
components, such as RNAs or proteins. 
• Mutations can result from the incorporation of incorrect bases during DNA 
replication. In addition, various chemical changes occur in DNA either 
spontaneously or as a result of exposure to chemicals or radiation. 
• To maintain the integrity of their genomes, cells have had to evolve mechanisms 
to repair damaged DNA. 
1) Direct reversal of the chemical reaction responsible for DNA damage 
2) Removal of the damaged bases followed by their replacement with newly 
synthesized DNA
3) Additional mechanisms to enable cells to cope with the damage

15

another.

in a variety of locations: upstream of genes, distant locations in the genome,

to regulate gene expression.

2. Proofreading by DNA polymerase
20
• The other mechanism is the proofreading activity of DNA 
polymerase. 
• Exonuclease activity of replicative DNA polymerases (III in

– hydrolyzes DNA in the 3′  5′ direction which operates

• The 3′  5′ exonucleases of DNA polymerases selectively

15
• Although introns are excised from completed mRNAs, they have many other 
important biological roles.

is critical to cell behavior.

gene expression determine the difference between one type of cell and 
another.
– Transcription is regulated by transcriptional regulatory sequences that reside 
in a variety of locations: upstream of genes, distant locations in the genome, 
or within genes (gene’s 1st intron or 5’ UTR of 1st exon). 
– Approximately 10–20% of the human genome consists of sequences that act 
to regulate gene expression.

candidates.full_text:
Amino acid sequence of insulin
• In 1953 Frederick Sanger was the first to determine the complete amino acid 
sequence of a protein, the hormone insulin.
• Insulin was found to consist of two polypeptide chains, joined by disulfide bonds 
between cysteine residues.
• Sanger’s experiment revealed that each protein consists of a specific amino acid 
sequence.
• Protein sequences are now usually deduced from the sequences of mRNAs, and 
the complete amino acid sequences of over 100,000 proteins have been 
established.

Comparison of velocity sedimentation and equilibrium 
sedimentation for the separation of subcellular particles. 
In velocity sedimentation, separation relies on different velocity of 
sedimentation through a shallow sucrose (or other material) 
gradient. The sucrose is added to prevent mixing by convection. 
In equilibrium sedimentation, subcellular particles sediment until

19
• One mechanism by which DNA polymerase increases the fidelity of replication is 
by helping to select the correct base for insertion into newly synthesized DNA.

Summary _The Structure of Eukaryotic Genes 
19
 Gene
 Exon, Intron
 RNA splicing
 5’ and 3’ UTR (untranslated region)
 Nested genes
 Transcriptional regulatory elements
 Alternative splicing
• Most eukaryotic genes have a split structure in which segments of coding sequence 
(exons) are interrupted by noncoding sequences (introns). 
• The exons include 5’ UTR and 3’ UTR regions at both the 5’ and 3’ ends of the mRNA 
that are not translated into protein, respectively. 
• Although they are removed from mRNAs, introns have multiple functions.
1. Some proteins or RNAs as nested genes are encoded within introns.
2. Introns contain transcriptional regulatory sequences that control gene expression.
3. Introns allow alternative splicing.

• Intron: noncoding sequences  intervening sequences 
(transcribed but not translated)

removed by splicing, so only exons are included in the messenger RNA (mRNA). 
 creates “mature transcripts”

Roles of introns (3)
17
• Although introns are excised from completed mRNAs, they have many other 
important biological roles. 
• Third, sequences within introns regulate splicing, which is critical to the formation 
of functional mRNAs. 
• The presence of introns allows the exons of a gene to be joined in different 
combinations, resulting in the synthesis of different proteins from the same gene. 
 Alternative splicing
– Approximately 90% of human genes can be alternatively spliced to yield 
between two and several thousand different mRNAs. 
– On average, each human gene yields six alternatively spliced mRNAs, four of 
which encode different proteins. 
– Alternative splicing thus allows the 20,000 human protein-coding genes to 
specify nearly 80,000 different proteins.

RNA Processing and Turnover

Splicing mechanism
-
Introns (noncoding sequences) are removed from pre-mRNA by splicing.
-
In mammals, most genes contain multiple introns.
-
Conserved sequences occur at the 5′ splice site, the 3′ splice site, and the branch point.

Splicing proceeds in two steps:

①
The branch-point A 2′-OH attacks the 5′ 
splice site (SS), forming a 2′–5′ bond 
and a lariat intermediate.

②
The 5′ exon 3′-OH attacks the 3′ SS, 
joining the exons and releasing the 
intron lariat.

important biological roles. 
• Second, introns contain regulatory sequences that control gene expression, which 
is critical to cell behavior. 
– Since all cells in an organism contain the same genes, regulated differences in 
gene expression determine the difference between one type of cell and 
another.
– Transcription is regulated by transcriptional regulatory sequences that reside 
in a variety of locations: upstream of genes, distant locations in the genome, 
or within genes (gene’s 1st intron or 5’ UTR of 1st exon). 
– Approximately 10–20% of the human genome consists of sequences that act 
to regulate gene expression.

14
• Chromosome is a long DNA molecule with genetic materials of an organism.
• Compared to prokaryotes, the genomes of most eukaryotes are much more complex 
and the DNA of eukaryotic cells is also well-organized. 
• Basic structure of chromosome in all eukaryotes
– DNA is tightly bound to small basic proteins (histones) that package the DNA in an orderly 
way in cell nucleus. 
– In a human cell, total DNA (2 m length) fits into a nucleus (5–10 μm diameter) 
Chromosome Numbers of Eukaryotic Cells
• Prokaryotes

• Eukaryotes
̶ multiple chromosomes

• Important points to understand DNA replication
1. Two complementary strands of double-helical DNA run in opposite

Summary and 
Key 
terms
25
• DNA polymerases synthesize DNA in the 5′  3′ direction by the addition of dNTP to a 
preformed RNA primer.
 The leading strand is synthesized in a continuous manner at the replication fork. 
 The lagging strand is formed by the joining of small Okazaki fragments that are synthesized 
backward of replication.
• DNA polymerases and various other proteins (helicase, primase, single-strand DNA-
binding proteins, clamp-loading protein, sliding-clamp proteins, topoisomerase) act in a 
coordinated manner to synthesize DNA. 
• DNA polymerases increase the accuracy of replication both by selecting the correct base
for insertion and by proofreading newly synthesized DNA to eliminate mismatched bases. 
• DNA replication starts at origins of replication, which contain binding sites for proteins 
that initiate the process. 
• Telomeric repeat sequences are maintained by the action of a reverse transcriptase 
(telomerase) that carries its own template RNA.

• During DNA replication, mismatched bases are removed by the proofreading 
activity of DNA polymerase.

The replication fidelity by DNA polymerase
18
• The free energy differences resulting from the changes in hydrogen bonding 
between matched and mismatched bases are large enough to favor the formation 
of correctly matched base pairs by 100-fold. 
• Consequently, base selection determined by hydrogen bonding between 
complementary bases result in an error frequency corresponding to one incorrect 
base incorporation in every 100 nucleotides of new DNA strand. 
• However, the error frequency during DNA replication corresponds to less than 
1/109 nucleotides incorporated and is much lower than would be predicted simply 
on the basis of complementary base pairing.
 The much higher degree of fidelity actually achieved results largely from the 
activities of DNA polymerase.

be corrected after replication is complete.

2.3. Mismatch repair 
8
• During DNA replication, mismatched bases are removed by the proofreading 
activity of DNA polymerase.
• However, the ones that are missed are subject to later correction by the 
mismatch repair system, which scans newly replicated DNA. 
 If a mismatch is found, the enzymes of the mismatch repair system are able 
to identify and excise the mismatched base specifically from the newly 
replicated DNA strand, allowing the error to be corrected and the original 
sequence restored.
• The mismatch repair system distinguishes between parental DNA and newly 
synthesized DNA.

and lack 3′  5′ proofreading activity.

1. Base selection by DNA polymerase
19
• One mechanism by which DNA polymerase increases the fidelity of replication is 
by helping to select the correct base for insertion into newly synthesized DNA.
• DNA polymerase actively discriminates against incorporation of a mismatched 
base by adapting to the conformation of a correct base pair.
• This ability of DNA polymerase to select matched nucleotides for incorporation 
increases the accuracy of replication about a 1000-fold.

candidates.full_text:
The replication fidelity by DNA polymerase
18
• The free energy differences resulting from the changes in hydrogen bonding 
between matched and mismatched bases are large enough to favor the formation 
of correctly matched base pairs by 100-fold. 
• Consequently, base selection determined by hydrogen bonding between 
complementary bases result in an error frequency corresponding to one incorrect 
base incorporation in every 100 nucleotides of new DNA strand. 
• However, the error frequency during DNA replication corresponds to less than 
1/109 nucleotides incorporated and is much lower than would be predicted simply 
on the basis of complementary base pairing.
 The much higher degree of fidelity actually achieved results largely from the 
activities of DNA polymerase.

questions.stem: 다음은 UV에 의한 DNA damage를 repair하는 direct reversal 과정이다. 빈칸 1, 2에 들어 갈 적당한 용어를 영어로 쓰시오. UV light induces thymine dimers in which adjacent thymines on the same DNA strand are joined by the formation of ( 1 ) with double bonds between carbons 5 and 6. The UV-induced thymine dimers are repaired by direct reversal called ( 2 ) because energy from visible light is used to break the double bonds. The original pyrimidine bases remain in DNA, now restored to their normal state.

다음은 Homologous recombination 과정이다. 빈칸 1, 2에 들어갈 적당한 용어를 쓰시오. Double-strand breaks occur naturally during DNA replication in E. coli. Both strands of DNA are first resected by nucleases in the ( 1 ) direction. ( 2 ) bind(s) to the overhanging 3′ single-stranded ends, which then invade the other parental DNA molecule and catalyze the exchange of strands between homologous sequences. The gaps are then filled by repair synthesis and sealed by ligation. Cleavage and ligation of the crossed strands finally yield recombinant molecules.

Key terms
28
• Programmed DNA rearrangements of immunoglobulin and T cell receptor genes 
play a critical role in development of the vertebrate immune system.
– Rearrangement of V(D)J regions in light and heavy chain of immunoglobulin. 
– Recombination between V(D)J segments in α and β chain of T cell receptor. 
– V(D)J recombination by RAG1/RAG2 introducing a double-strand break 
between the V(D) coding sequence and RS sequence, accompanied by 
nonhomologous end-joining and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase for 
nucleotide deletions and additions, respectively.
• Additional diversity is provided to immunoglobulin genes by class switch 
recombination and somatic hypermutation.

Telomeres and telomerase
23
• Because DNA polymerases extend primers only in the 5′  3′ direction, they are 
unable to copy the extreme 5′ ends of linear DNA in eukaryotes. 
• Telomeres consist of tandem repeats of simple-sequence DNA and are maintained 
by the action of telomerase.
– A reverse transcriptase, one of a class of DNA polymerases, first discovered in 
retroviruses that synthesize DNA from an RNA template.
– Telomerase carries its own template RNA, which is complementary to the 
telomere repeat sequences. This template RNA allows to generate multiple 
copies of the telomeric repeat sequences, thereby maintaining telomeres in 
the absence of DNA template.
• Finally, the ends of eukaryotic chromosomes are replicated by a special reverse 
transcriptase (telomerase).

Translation of mRNA

Genetic code: The rules by which the nucleotide sequence of a gene,

through an intermediary mRNA molecule, is translated into the amino 
acid sequence of a protein.

- the sequence of nucleotides in an mRNA molecule is read consecutively in groups of

three
- because RNA is made of 4 different nucleotides, there are 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 possible

combinations of three nucleotides: AAA, AUA, AUG, and so on
- However, only 20 different amino acids are commonly found in proteins

some amino acids being specified by more than one triplet

Codon: a three-nucleotide unit specifying an amino acid or a stop signal

-
Usual start codon: AUG (alternative starts also occur)
-
Stop codons: UAA, UAG, and UGA

established.

Regulation of transcriptional elongation (Figure 7.17)
CTD: 7aa-52 in human
Transcription is initiated following 
phosphorylation of the RNA 
polymerase II C-terminal domain 
(CTD) at serine-5 by TFIIH.
Factors involved in the initial stages 
of mRNA processing associate with 
the phosphorylated CTD. 
In addition, negative regulatory 
factors (NELF and DSIF) associate 
with the polymerase and cause the 
polymerase to pause within about 50 
nucleotides of the transcription start 
site. DRB sensitivity-inducing factor
Continuation of transcription 
(productive elongation) results from 
the phosphorylation of NELF, DSIF, 
and serine-2 of the polymerase CTD 
by P-TEFb. Phosphorylated NELF 
dissociates from the complex, and 
additional factors required for 
elongation and processing associate 
with the polymerase.
‘stalled’(정체/멈춤)
‘poised’(준비된/대기 상태)
‘paused’(일시정지)

accuracy of replication by 100~1000-fold.

Molecular biology terminology
6
• Gene: a segment of DNA that is expressed to yield a functional product, RNA or 
polypeptide.
• Each protein-coding gene is used to produce RNA molecules (transcription), 
which then direct the production of the specific protein molecules (translation).
• Exon: protein-coding sequence  expressed sequences 
(translated into amino acid sequence)
• Intron: noncoding sequences  intervening sequences 
(transcribed but not translated)
• The entire gene is transcribed to yield a long RNA molecule and the introns are then 
removed by splicing, so only exons are included in the messenger RNA (mRNA). 
 creates “mature transcripts”

원론적으로 모든 화학반응은 가역반응

•Reversible systems occur in situations when the system is in equilibrium

Chemical Reversible Reaction (화학적 가역반응): 
정반응과 역반응이 모두 가능하고, 시간이 지나면 동적 평형(정·역 반응 
속도가 같음)에 도달하는 반응
원론적으로 모든 화학반응은 가역반응
비가역반응 사례 (생성물이 반응계에서 제거되어 역반응에 참여할 수 
없거나 참여하여도 너무 느리고 약하기 때문)
1)이온 결합물질의 침전 (앙금 생성)
2)강산 + 강염기의 중화반응
3)기체 생성반응
화학적 가역반응은 두 방향으로 진행될 수 있다는 뜻이며, 열역학적 의
미의 “가역과정(엔트로피 변화를 전혀 생산하지 않는 이상화된 과정)”
을 뜻하는 것은 아님. 
Definition in chemical reaction (II)
13
열역학적 가역과정 (Thermodynamically Reversible Process)
•A change in a system that can be undone by doing the exact opposite of 
what you did. 
ex) melting or freezing ice at 00C (at equilibrium)
•Reversible systems occur in situations when the system is in equilibrium 
during the transition, and only an infinitesimal amount of work would 
be necessary to truly restore equilibrium.
•An idealized process in which entropy is exchanged between a system
and its surroundings and no net change of entropy is generated 
(dSgen= 0). 
•Spontaneous process is nota reversible process.

Roles of introns (3)
17
• Although introns are excised from completed mRNAs, they have many other 
important biological roles. 
• Third, sequences within introns regulate splicing, which is critical to the formation 
of functional mRNAs. 
• The presence of introns allows the exons of a gene to be joined in different 
combinations, resulting in the synthesis of different proteins from the same gene. 
 Alternative splicing
– Approximately 90% of human genes can be alternatively spliced to yield 
between two and several thousand different mRNAs. 
– On average, each human gene yields six alternatively spliced mRNAs, four of 
which encode different proteins. 
– Alternative splicing thus allows the 20,000 human protein-coding genes to 
specify nearly 80,000 different proteins.

14
• Chromosome is a long DNA molecule with genetic materials of an organism.
• Compared to prokaryotes, the genomes of most eukaryotes are much more complex 
and the DNA of eukaryotic cells is also well-organized. 
• Basic structure of chromosome in all eukaryotes
– DNA is tightly bound to small basic proteins (histones) that package the DNA in an orderly 
way in cell nucleus. 
– In a human cell, total DNA (2 m length) fits into a nucleus (5–10 μm diameter) 
Chromosome Numbers of Eukaryotic Cells
• Prokaryotes

̶ usually circular DNA molecules
• Eukaryotes
̶ multiple chromosomes 
̶ each contains a linear DNA molecule

RNA Processing and Turnover

Splicing mechanism
-
Introns (noncoding sequences) are removed from pre-mRNA by splicing.
-
In mammals, most genes contain multiple introns.
-
Conserved sequences occur at the 5′ splice site, the 3′ splice site, and the branch point.

Splicing proceeds in two steps:

①
The branch-point A 2′-OH attacks the 5′ 
splice site (SS), forming a 2′–5′ bond 
and a lariat intermediate.

②
The 5′ exon 3′-OH attacks the 3′ SS, 
joining the exons and releasing the 
intron lariat.

Summary _The Structure of Eukaryotic Genes 
19
 Gene
 Exon, Intron
 RNA splicing
 5’ and 3’ UTR (untranslated region)
 Nested genes
 Transcriptional regulatory elements
 Alternative splicing
• Most eukaryotic genes have a split structure in which segments of coding sequence 
(exons) are interrupted by noncoding sequences (introns). 
• The exons include 5’ UTR and 3’ UTR regions at both the 5’ and 3’ ends of the mRNA 
that are not translated into protein, respectively. 
• Although they are removed from mRNAs, introns have multiple functions.
1. Some proteins or RNAs as nested genes are encoded within introns.
2. Introns contain transcriptional regulatory sequences that control gene expression.
3. Introns allow alternative splicing.

candidates.full_text:
Mechanism of gene duplication
9
• Gene duplication is the process of creating additional copies of a gene within an 
organism's genome through various mechanisms, such as retrotransposition.
• Duplication of DNA segment
– The transfer of a block of DNA sequence to a new location in genome
– Duplications of 1 ~ 50 kb DNA segments are estimated to account for 
approximately 5% of the human genome. 
• Duplications of the entire genome 
– Particularly common in plants (e.g., Arabidopsis)
– Whole sequence has undergone at least two full-genome duplications, followed 
by the gradual loss of some of the duplicated genes. 
– 26,000 protein-coding genes in Arabidopsis is the result of these duplications.

The replication fidelity by DNA polymerase
18
• The free energy differences resulting from the changes in hydrogen bonding 
between matched and mismatched bases are large enough to favor the formation 
of correctly matched base pairs by 100-fold. 
• Consequently, base selection determined by hydrogen bonding between 
complementary bases result in an error frequency corresponding to one incorrect 
base incorporation in every 100 nucleotides of new DNA strand. 
• However, the error frequency during DNA replication corresponds to less than 
1/109 nucleotides incorporated and is much lower than would be predicted simply 
on the basis of complementary base pairing.
 The much higher degree of fidelity actually achieved results largely from the 
activities of DNA polymerase.

top_match.full_text:
Summary and 
Key terms
17
• Direct reversal repair is to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers on the same DNA 
strand by photoreactivation using energy from visible light.
• Base-excision repair is to recognize specific lesions (deamination) and repair at AP 
(apyrimidinic or apurinic) site. 
• Nucleotide-excision repair is to recognize and remove an oligonucleotide 
containing the lesion. 
• Mismatch repair distinguishes between parental DNA and newly synthesized DNA 
and specifically removes mismatched bases from newly synthesized DNA strands. 
• Translesion DNA synthesis repairs lesions by specialized DNA polymerases that are 
capable of replicating DNA across from a site of DNA damage.
• Double-strand breaks are repaired by recombination to rejoin the damaged 
strands, either by nonhomologous end joining of the broken ends or by 
homologous recombination with an undamaged chromosome.

candidates.full_text:
Molecular biology terminology
6
• Gene: a segment of DNA that is expressed to yield a functional product, RNA or 
polypeptide.
• Each protein-coding gene is used to produce RNA molecules (transcription), 
which then direct the production of the specific protein molecules (translation).
• Exon: protein-coding sequence  expressed sequences 
(translated into amino acid sequence)
• Intron: noncoding sequences  intervening sequences 
(transcribed but not translated)
• The entire gene is transcribed to yield a long RNA molecule and the introns are then 
removed by splicing, so only exons are included in the messenger RNA (mRNA). 
 creates “mature transcripts”

Molecular biology terminology
6
• Gene: a segment of DNA that is expressed to yield a functional product, RNA or 
polypeptide.
• Each protein-coding gene is used to produce RNA molecules (transcription), 
which then direct the production of the specific protein molecules (translation).
• Exon: protein-coding sequence  expressed sequences 
(translated into amino acid sequence)
• Intron: noncoding sequences  intervening sequences 
(transcribed but not translated)
• The entire gene is transcribed to yield a long RNA molecule and the introns are then 
removed by splicing, so only exons are included in the messenger RNA (mRNA). 
 creates “mature transcripts”

• Although they are removed from mRNAs, introns have multiple functions.

candidates.full_text:
Roles of introns (2)
15
• Although introns are excised from completed mRNAs, they have many other 
important biological roles. 
• Second, introns contain regulatory sequences that control gene expression, which 
is critical to cell behavior. 
– Since all cells in an organism contain the same genes, regulated differences in 
gene expression determine the difference between one type of cell and 
another.
– Transcription is regulated by transcriptional regulatory sequences that reside 
in a variety of locations: upstream of genes, distant locations in the genome, 
or within genes (gene’s 1st intron or 5’ UTR of 1st exon). 
– Approximately 10–20% of the human genome consists of sequences that act 
to regulate gene expression.

Chromatin
15
• Chromatin: The complexes between eukaryotic DNA and proteins, which typically 
contains about twice as much protein as DNA. 
• Histones: The major proteins of chromatin 
– Small proteins containing a high proportion of basic amino acids (lysine and arginine) 
that facilitate binding to the negatively charged DNA molecule. 
• Nonhistone chromosomal proteins: an equal mass in chromatin 
– involved in a range of activities (e. g., DNA replication and gene expression) 
– very similar among different 
species of eukaryotes. 
– equal mass to that of the cell’s DNA

Ribosome: a molecular machine that can move along the mRNA, capture

covalently link the amino acids that they carry to form a polypeptide chain

- Sedimentation coefficients: bacterial 70S and eukaryotic cytosolic 80S. S values are not

additive.
- All ribosomes have two subunits which contain rRNA and characteristic proteins

E (exit), P (peptidyl), and A 
(aminoacyl) sites of the ribosome

Chromosomes
14
• Chromosome is a long DNA molecule with genetic materials of an organism.
• Compared to prokaryotes, the genomes of most eukaryotes are much more complex 
and the DNA of eukaryotic cells is also well-organized. 
• Basic structure of chromosome in all eukaryotes
– DNA is tightly bound to small basic proteins (histones) that package the DNA in an orderly 
way in cell nucleus. 
– In a human cell, total DNA (2 m length) fits into a nucleus (5–10 μm diameter) 
Chromosome Numbers of Eukaryotic Cells
• Prokaryotes
̶ single chromosome
̶ usually circular DNA molecules
• Eukaryotes
̶ multiple chromosomes 
̶ each contains a linear DNA molecule

Summary and 
Key 
terms
25
• DNA polymerases synthesize DNA in the 5′  3′ direction by the addition of dNTP to a 
preformed RNA primer.
 The leading strand is synthesized in a continuous manner at the replication fork. 
 The lagging strand is formed by the joining of small Okazaki fragments that are synthesized 
backward of replication.
• DNA polymerases and various other proteins (helicase, primase, single-strand DNA-
binding proteins, clamp-loading protein, sliding-clamp proteins, topoisomerase) act in a 
coordinated manner to synthesize DNA. 
• DNA polymerases increase the accuracy of replication both by selecting the correct base
for insertion and by proofreading newly synthesized DNA to eliminate mismatched bases. 
• DNA replication starts at origins of replication, which contain binding sites for proteins 
that initiate the process.

Summary and 
Key terms
17
• Direct reversal repair is to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers on the same DNA 
strand by photoreactivation using energy from visible light.

(apyrimidinic or apurinic) site.

containing the lesion.

and specifically removes mismatched bases from newly synthesized DNA strands. 
• Translesion DNA synthesis repairs lesions by specialized DNA polymerases that are 
capable of replicating DNA across from a site of DNA damage.

strands, either by nonhomologous end joining of the broken ends or by 
homologous recombination with an undamaged chromosome.

• Most eukaryotic genes have a split structure in which segments of coding sequence

Velocity centrifugation: Size, Shape
Equilibrium centrifugation: Density
Comparison of velocity sedimentation and equilibrium 
sedimentation for the separation of subcellular particles. 
In velocity sedimentation, separation relies on different velocity of 
sedimentation through a shallow sucrose (or other material) 
gradient. The sucrose is added to prevent mixing by convection. 
In equilibrium sedimentation, subcellular particles sediment until 
they reach a zone of solution that matches their density. At 
equilibrium, the organelles distribute themselves over a narrow 
region of the tube corresponding to the density of the organelle. 
The organelles can then be harvested from a narrow band.

The replication fidelity by DNA polymerase
18
• The free energy differences resulting from the changes in hydrogen bonding 
between matched and mismatched bases are large enough to favor the formation 
of correctly matched base pairs by 100-fold. 
• Consequently, base selection determined by hydrogen bonding between 
complementary bases result in an error frequency corresponding to one incorrect 
base incorporation in every 100 nucleotides of new DNA strand. 
• However, the error frequency during DNA replication corresponds to less than 
1/109 nucleotides incorporated and is much lower than would be predicted simply 
on the basis of complementary base pairing.
 The much higher degree of fidelity actually achieved results largely from the 
activities of DNA polymerase.

top_match.full_text:
Summary and 
Key terms
17
• Direct reversal repair is to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers on the same DNA 
strand by photoreactivation using energy from visible light.
• Base-excision repair is to recognize specific lesions (deamination) and repair at AP 
(apyrimidinic or apurinic) site. 
• Nucleotide-excision repair is to recognize and remove an oligonucleotide 
containing the lesion. 
• Mismatch repair distinguishes between parental DNA and newly synthesized DNA 
and specifically removes mismatched bases from newly synthesized DNA strands. 
• Translesion DNA synthesis repairs lesions by specialized DNA polymerases that are 
capable of replicating DNA across from a site of DNA damage.
• Double-strand breaks are repaired by recombination to rejoin the damaged 
strands, either by nonhomologous end joining of the broken ends or by 
homologous recombination with an undamaged chromosome.

Molecular biology terminology
6
• Gene: a segment of DNA that is expressed to yield a functional product, RNA or 
polypeptide.
• Each protein-coding gene is used to produce RNA molecules (transcription), 
which then direct the production of the specific protein molecules (translation).
• Exon: protein-coding sequence  expressed sequences 
(translated into amino acid sequence)
• Intron: noncoding sequences  intervening sequences 
(transcribed but not translated)
• The entire gene is transcribed to yield a long RNA molecule and the introns are then 
removed by splicing, so only exons are included in the messenger RNA (mRNA). 
 creates “mature transcripts”

Summary and 
Key terms
28
• Programmed DNA rearrangements of immunoglobulin and T cell receptor genes 
play a critical role in development of the vertebrate immune system.
– Rearrangement of V(D)J regions in light and heavy chain of immunoglobulin. 
– Recombination between V(D)J segments in α and β chain of T cell receptor. 
– V(D)J recombination by RAG1/RAG2 introducing a double-strand break 
between the V(D) coding sequence and RS sequence, accompanied by 
nonhomologous end-joining and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase for 
nucleotide deletions and additions, respectively.
• Additional diversity is provided to immunoglobulin genes by class switch 
recombination and somatic hypermutation.

Summary and 
Key terms
28
• Programmed DNA rearrangements of immunoglobulin and T cell receptor genes 
play a critical role in development of the vertebrate immune system.
– Rearrangement of V(D)J regions in light and heavy chain of immunoglobulin. 
– Recombination between V(D)J segments in α and β chain of T cell receptor. 
– V(D)J recombination by RAG1/RAG2 introducing a double-strand break 
between the V(D) coding sequence and RS sequence, accompanied by 
nonhomologous end-joining and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase for 
nucleotide deletions and additions, respectively.
• Additional diversity is provided to immunoglobulin genes by class switch 
recombination and somatic hypermutation.

How can DNA strand be synthesized?
7
• Important points to understand DNA replication
1. Two complementary strands of double-helical DNA run in opposite 
(antiparallel) directions. 
2. DNA polymerase catalyzes the polymerization of dNTPs only in the 5′ to 3′ 
direction. 
• One strand is synthesized in a continuous manner in the same direction in 
which the replication fork moves (in the direction of overall DNA replication) 
 the leading strand
• The other strand is formed from short (1–3 kb), discontinuous pieces of DNA 
that are synthesized backward to the direction of replication fork movement 
 the lagging strand
– Okazaki fragments: Small pieces of newly synthesized DNA 
– DNA ligase: join Okazaki fragments and form a new intact DNA strand

2. Proofreading by DNA polymerase
20
• The other mechanism is the proofreading activity of DNA 
polymerase. 
• Exonuclease activity of replicative DNA polymerases (III in 
E.coli, δ and ε in eukaryotes)
– hydrolyzes DNA in the 3′  5′ direction which operates 
in the reverse direction of DNA synthesis, and 
participates in proofreading newly synthesized DNA.
• The 3′  5′ exonucleases of DNA polymerases selectively 
excise mismatched bases that have been incorporated at 
the end of a growing DNA chain, thereby increasing the 
accuracy of replication by 100~1000-fold.

2.3. Mismatch repair 
8
• During DNA replication, mismatched bases are removed by the proofreading 
activity of DNA polymerase.
• However, the ones that are missed are subject to later correction by the 
mismatch repair system, which scans newly replicated DNA. 
 If a mismatch is found, the enzymes of the mismatch repair system are able 
to identify and excise the mismatched base specifically from the newly 
replicated DNA strand, allowing the error to be corrected and the original 
sequence restored.
• The mismatch repair system distinguishes between parental DNA and newly 
synthesized DNA.

Summary and 
Key 
terms
25
• DNA polymerases synthesize DNA in the 5′  3′ direction by the addition of dNTP to a 
preformed RNA primer.
 The leading strand is synthesized in a continuous manner at the replication fork. 
 The lagging strand is formed by the joining of small Okazaki fragments that are synthesized 
backward of replication.
• DNA polymerases and various other proteins (helicase, primase, single-strand DNA-
binding proteins, clamp-loading protein, sliding-clamp proteins, topoisomerase) act in a 
coordinated manner to synthesize DNA. 
• DNA polymerases increase the accuracy of replication both by selecting the correct base
for insertion and by proofreading newly synthesized DNA to eliminate mismatched bases. 
• DNA replication starts at origins of replication, which contain binding sites for proteins 
that initiate the process. 
• Telomeric repeat sequences are maintained by the action of a reverse transcriptase 
(telomerase) that carries its own template RNA.

17

strands, either by nonhomologous end joining of the broken ends or by 
homologous recombination with an undamaged chromosome.

Homologous recombination
16
• Double-strand breaks can be repaired by 
homologous recombination with DNA sequences 
on an undamaged chromosome.
Both strands of DNA at double-strand break are resected 
by 5′  3′ nucleases, yielding overhanging 3′ single-
stranded ends.
The single strands are bound by the key protein, 
recombinase (RecA in E.coli, Rad51 in eukaryotes) involved 
in homologous recombination.
RecA-DNA filaments invade and bind a second, double-
stranded DNA molecule, and RecA catalyzes the exchange 
of strands between homologous sequences.
The gaps are filled by repair synthesis, and the strands are 
joined by ligation to yield a recombinant molecule.

• During DNA replication, mismatched bases are removed by the proofreading 
activity of DNA polymerase.
• However, the ones that are missed are subject to later correction by the 
mismatch repair system, which scans newly replicated DNA. 
 If a mismatch is found, the enzymes of the mismatch repair system are able 
to identify and excise the mismatched base specifically from the newly 
replicated DNA strand, allowing the error to be corrected and the original 
sequence restored.
• The mismatch repair system distinguishes between parental DNA and newly 
synthesized DNA.

strands, either by nonhomologous end joining of the broken ends or by 
homologous recombination with an undamaged chromosome.

candidates.full_text:
Mechanism of gene duplication
9
• Gene duplication is the process of creating additional copies of a gene within an 
organism's genome through various mechanisms, such as retrotransposition.
• Duplication of DNA segment
– The transfer of a block of DNA sequence to a new location in genome
– Duplications of 1 ~ 50 kb DNA segments are estimated to account for 
approximately 5% of the human genome. 
• Duplications of the entire genome 
– Particularly common in plants (e.g., Arabidopsis)
– Whole sequence has undergone at least two full-genome duplications, followed 
by the gradual loss of some of the duplicated genes. 
– 26,000 protein-coding genes in Arabidopsis is the result of these duplications.

DNA repair
3
• Because DNA uniquely serves as a permanent copy of the cell genome, changes in 
its structure are of much greater consequence than are alterations in other cell 
components, such as RNAs or proteins. 
• Mutations can result from the incorporation of incorrect bases during DNA 
replication. In addition, various chemical changes occur in DNA either 
spontaneously or as a result of exposure to chemicals or radiation. 
• To maintain the integrity of their genomes, cells have had to evolve mechanisms 
to repair damaged DNA. 
1) Direct reversal of the chemical reaction responsible for DNA damage 
2) Removal of the damaged bases followed by their replacement with newly 
synthesized DNA
3) Additional mechanisms to enable cells to cope with the damage

Summary and 
Key terms
17
• Direct reversal repair is to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers on the same DNA 
strand by photoreactivation using energy from visible light.
• Base-excision repair is to recognize specific lesions (deamination) and repair at AP 
(apyrimidinic or apurinic) site. 
• Nucleotide-excision repair is to recognize and remove an oligonucleotide 
containing the lesion. 
• Mismatch repair distinguishes between parental DNA and newly synthesized DNA 
and specifically removes mismatched bases from newly synthesized DNA strands. 
• Translesion DNA synthesis repairs lesions by specialized DNA polymerases that are 
capable of replicating DNA across from a site of DNA damage.
• Double-strand breaks are repaired by recombination to rejoin the damaged 
strands, either by nonhomologous end joining of the broken ends or by 
homologous recombination with an undamaged chromosome.

DNA repair
3
• Because DNA uniquely serves as a permanent copy of the cell genome, changes in 
its structure are of much greater consequence than are alterations in other cell 
components, such as RNAs or proteins. 
• Mutations can result from the incorporation of incorrect bases during DNA 
replication. In addition, various chemical changes occur in DNA either 
spontaneously or as a result of exposure to chemicals or radiation. 
• To maintain the integrity of their genomes, cells have had to evolve mechanisms 
to repair damaged DNA. 
1) Direct reversal of the chemical reaction responsible for DNA damage 
2) Removal of the damaged bases followed by their replacement with newly 
synthesized DNA
3) Additional mechanisms to enable cells to cope with the damage

intron lariat.

Regulation of transcriptional elongation (Figure 7.17)
CTD: 7aa-52 in human
Transcription is initiated following 
phosphorylation of the RNA 
polymerase II C-terminal domain 
(CTD) at serine-5 by TFIIH.
Factors involved in the initial stages 
of mRNA processing associate with 
the phosphorylated CTD. 
In addition, negative regulatory 
factors (NELF and DSIF) associate 
with the polymerase and cause the 
polymerase to pause within about 50 
nucleotides of the transcription start 
site. DRB sensitivity-inducing factor
Continuation of transcription 
(productive elongation) results from 
the phosphorylation of NELF, DSIF, 
and serine-2 of the polymerase CTD 
by P-TEFb. Phosphorylated NELF 
dissociates from the complex, and 
additional factors required for 
elongation and processing associate 
with the polymerase.

candidates.full_text:
Summary _The Structure of Eukaryotic Genes 
19
 Gene
 Exon, Intron
 RNA splicing
 5’ and 3’ UTR (untranslated region)
 Nested genes
 Transcriptional regulatory elements
 Alternative splicing
• Most eukaryotic genes have a split structure in which segments of coding sequence 
(exons) are interrupted by noncoding sequences (introns). 
• The exons include 5’ UTR and 3’ UTR regions at both the 5’ and 3’ ends of the mRNA 
that are not translated into protein, respectively. 
• Although they are removed from mRNAs, introns have multiple functions.
1. Some proteins or RNAs as nested genes are encoded within introns.
2. Introns contain transcriptional regulatory sequences that control gene expression.
3. Introns allow alternative splicing.

candidates.full_text:
RNA Processing and Turnover

“Regulation of processing provides another level of control of gene expression.”

Processing of ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs)
-
In many bacteria, 16S, 23S, and 5S rRNAs are processed from one common precursor.
-
In eukaryotes, 18S, 5.8S, and 28S rRNAs share a common precursor.
-
The fourth eukaryotic rRNA, 5S, is transcribed separately by RNA polymerase III.
